governance_posts.title: Aave Labs 180 Day Report
governance_posts.description:
Summary

Aave governance approved the Aave Will Win Framework in April 2026, and as part of that framework Aave Labs committed to publishing quarterly updates on its work as a service provider to the Aave DAO. This report combines the first the 180 days since that approval, spanning Q2 and Q3 2026.

Over the last 180 days, Aave Labs’ team of about 97 team members put an estimated 100,000 hours into its work for the Aave DAO and completed 6,096 tracked issues and 36 projects of various scopes across engineering, security, product, design, growth, marketing, governance, and legal. Over the same period, Aave Labs authored 26 onchain governance proposals and 20 Snapshot votes, and shipped 28 items including products, features, and protocol deployments. Aave Labs also prepared and implemented the DAO-approved onboarding of 33 unique assets, deployments on four new chains, and four new Aave V4 Liquidity Hubs with their corresponding Spokes.

Throughout Q2, Aave Labs assumed roughly 40 technical and supporting functions that BGD Labs and the Aave Chan Initiative (ACI) previously performed for the DAO, including contract maintenance, security coordination, proposal payload engineering, and developer tooling, and it completed both transitions while rsETH incident response (detailed below) was still underway.

Q3 was a strong quarter for launches and product expansion across the Aave ecosystem. Following DAO approval, Aave Labs implemented Aave V4 deployments on Avalanche, Arc, and Base, and V4 grew from $212.6 million deposits to $1.34 billion in Q3, passing its first $1 billion on September 16. Since launching from zero at the end of March, V4 has grown to more than $1.3 billion deposits in roughly six months. Aave App opened early access on iOS, expanded to five total chains, and launched instant onramps for eligible U.S. users through licensed third-party providers. We also opened up Stable Vaults, the vault infrastructure behind the Aave App, for enterprise use. Other key launches include the official Aave MCP server, which gives AI a direct connection to read Aave data and prepare transactions, the Aave V3 interface redesign, and the addition of each new V4 deployment to Aave Pro.

On the security side, Certora completed formal verification of core Aave V4 and Stable Vaults contracts against defined specifications, and three new V4 security audits were published over the period. Aave Labs coordinated these engagements, including scoping, remediation of findings, and fix review, before the final reports were published.

Aave Labs’ UK subsidiaries Push Labs Limited and Push Virtual Assets Limited (together, Push) were also registered with the Financial Conduct Authority as cryptoasset exchange providers. Push provides fiat on- and off-ramp services for eligible Aave App users.

Aave protocol revenue totaled $44.58 million across the 180 days, while deposits across all versions of the protocol grew by $9.69 billion in Q3 alone.

rsETH Response

On April 18 at 17:35 UTC, an exploit of the rsETH cross-chain bridge resulted in the release of 116,500 rsETH on Ethereum without a matching amount being burned on the source chain. The exploit did not involve the Aave Protocol’s smart contracts, which continued to operate as designed. The attacker supplied 89,567 of the stolen rsETH across eight Aave V3 positions and borrowed 82,650 WETH and 821 wstETH against it, after which the Aave Protocol Guardian froze the affected reserves within 85 minutes and the Risk Stewards made roughly 295 parameter changes across V3 reserves over the following weeks to contain exposure.

Aave Labs, TokenLogic, and LlamaRisk then helped coordinate DeFi United, a cross-protocol effort to restore rsETH’s backing for affected users. Within a week, Consensys and Joseph Lubin committed up to 30,000 ETH with strategic advice from SharpLink, Aave service providers proposed that Aave DAO contribute 25,000 ETH, and Golem contributed 1,000 ETH, while EtherFi, Ethena, Mantle, Frax, the Ink Foundation, Tydro, and LayerZero also joined the effort.

On April 25, Aave service providers, together with EtherFi, Kelp, LayerZero, Compound, and others, submitted a proposal asking the Arbitrum DAO to release into the recovery the ETH that the Arbitrum Security Council had frozen after the exploit. The vote reached quorum with more than 1,600 addresses representing over 190 million ARB. On May 1, a restraining notice was issued against the Arbitrum DAO in connection with an unrelated case. Following an application by Aave LLC, the court modified the notice on May 8 to allow the onchain vote and the transfer of the ETH to Aave LLC.

Aave governance executed AIP 478 on May 6, which liquidated the eight attacker positions without affecting any other users or Umbrella, Aave’s staking-based backstop. AIP 482 followed on May 16 and restored WETH borrowing limits to their pre-incident levels across the V3 Ethereum Core, Ethereum Prime, Arbitrum, Base, Mantle, and Linea markets. Kelp refilled the bridge with recovered rsETH across five tranches totaling 116,131.72 rsETH, which fully restored rsETH’s backing by May 26 and returned all Aave markets to normal operation.

Aave Labs prioritized its incident response work over its launch schedule and moved the affected launches into Q3. The public post mortem gives a fuller account of the response.

DAO Launches Overview

Aave Labs authored 26 onchain proposals and 20 Snapshot votes over the 180 days, and it submitted another 16 onchain proposals on behalf of other service providers. Onchain proposals are binding votes that execute code on the protocol, and Snapshot votes are offchain votes the DAO uses to approve a direction before the onchain step.

Aave Labs submitted the other 16 proposals in collaboration with TokenLogic, LlamaRisk, Chaos Labs, and Certora as part of the payload engineering function it took over from BGD Labs. A payload is the smart contract code that a proposal executes, and Aave Labs now writes, tests, and submits that code for other service providers in addition to its own proposals.

Aave Labs also published the Technical Asset Listing Framework to the governance forum on May 28, which sets one technical standard for every new asset listing, continued listing, and material parameter expansion across Aave V3, Aave V4, and Aave Horizon, along with requirements for ongoing monitoring of listed assets. The framework passed Snapshot in July and is now a formal part of the asset onboarding process.

Eight came through standalone listing proposals, and 25 launched with the four new chain deployments. Functions Absorbed from BGD Labs and ACI

During Q2, Aave Labs assumed roughly 40 technical and supporting functions from BGD Labs and ACI (with others taken on by TokenLogic), spanning developer tooling, security coordination, and governance infrastructure. Aave Labs now maintains the Aave Address Book, which is the official registry of every Aave contract address and deployment, the Aave Helpers, which are shared code libraries used across proposals, the Aave CLI, which is the command-line toolkit developers use to build on Aave, and the Aave Permission Book, which publicly documents the addresses that hold permissions on the protocol.

Aave Labs is also adapting the Correlated Assets Price Oracle (CAPO) to V4. CAPO limits how quickly the price of a yield-bearing asset such as wstETH can rise, which protects Aave markets from price manipulation.

Through the same transition, Aave Labs took on security coordination and vulnerability response support for V3 and earlier versions, along with ongoing contract maintenance for those versions and the deprecation of the legacy Safety Module. Aave Labs now prepares the technical deployment work for DAO-approved asset listings and chain launches across protocol versions, which over this period included the V3 Monad market and the V4 Avalanche, Arc, and Base deployments.

Aave V4

Aave V4 passed $1 billion deposits on September 16 and reached a high of $1.41 billion on October 12. Over the 180 days, V4 expanded from Ethereum to three more chains, with four new Liquidity Hubs and seven new markets approved by the DAO and implemented by Aave Labs, while deposits grew in every month of the period and active loans passed $400 million on September 29.

Aave V4 went live on Avalanche on July 15, which made it the first V4 deployment outside Ethereum, and the deployment passed $30 million deposits on September 23. On September 16, Aave Labs announced that V4’s first RWA Hub, a market where institutions can borrow against tokenized real-world assets, is planned to launch on Avalanche, subject to governance approval, with Tether’s USA₮ as its main source of dollar liquidity.

On August 14, EtherFi moved the credit backend for EtherFi Cash to a dedicated Aave V4 instance on Optimism, which lets more than 100,000 cardholders borrow against PAXG, SPYx, WBTC, ETH, and ETHFI. The instance passed $100 million deposits in its first week. EtherFi manages the instance itself, outside Aave DAO governance, and it shares a portion of its revenue with Aave DAO.

Sentora published an ARFC on September 28 for an externally curated Hub and Spoke framework on V4, under which Sentora would run its own Liquidity Hub on Ethereum with RLUSD Yield, OUSD Yield, and Bluechip markets at launch and a PYUSD Yield market planned later. Sentora sets collateral, risk parameters, interest rate curves, liquidation settings, and oracles, while the Aave DAO Governance Short Executor keeps ownership of the contracts and admin roles, and any change that increases risk would wait 48 hours behind an onchain timelock. Aave DAO receives 50 percent of the instance’s protocol revenue.

Babylon Integration

Native BTC loans, powered by Babylon’s Trustless Vaults, ran on V4 testnet in June, and the integration is now in audit with Certora, two independent researchers, and an internal Aave Labs review. Bringing native Bitcoin to V4 would unlock much more BTC collateral for Aave than currently exists inside the wrapped versions of the asset.

V4-Specific Security and Risk Management

Aave Labs’ smart contract security team led the security work on V4 over the 180 days. Alongside external audits, the team introduced AI-assisted code review across Aave Labs repositories and coordinated each external engagement through scoping, remediation, and fix review.

Aave Labs worked with Certora to formally verify the core V4 contracts in July, covering the Liquidity Hub, the Spoke, and the Tokenization Spoke contracts along with the math libraries they rely on. Formal verification uses mathematical proofs to check that code behaves according to a defined set of specifications. Aave Labs also worked with Sherlock on a new V4 security audit published May 26, and with ChainSecurity on two more, one on the Tokenization Spoke published June 19 and one on the Liquidity Hub, Spoke, and position manager contracts published July 21.

AIP 523, authored by Aave Labs and approved by the DAO, activated Risk Stewards on V4 on September 25. Risk Stewards allow risk service providers to raise or lower supply caps, borrow caps, and other risk settings within preset limits and waiting periods, so V4 can adjust to demand within days, with no separate DAO vote needed for each change.

Aave Labs also worked to integrate Chainlink SVR into Aave V4 markets for eligible assets. SVR, short for Smart Value Recapture, captures the profit that bots earn from liquidations and returns it to the DAO, and on V3 it has returned over $11 million to the DAO treasury since March 2025.

Aave App

Aave App opened to its first users through Ghost Passes on August 26, and since then users from around the world have started using the app, funding it with stablecoins or from their bank accounts through Push and licensed providers. Balances across all Aave App users have since crossed $45 million.

During Q3, Aave Labs added instant deposit onboarding for eligible U.S. users, provided through licensed providers, and expanded Aave App from one chain to five, adding Ethereum, Base, HyperEVM, and BNB Chain to Arbitrum so users can deposit stablecoins from any of those networks. Aave Labs also spent Q3 developing the Android version of the app, which we currently expect to complete in the coming months.

During the period, Aave Labs’ UK subsidiaries Push Labs Limited and Push Virtual Assets Limited were registered with the Financial Conduct Authority as cryptoasset exchange providers under the Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017.

Aave Pro

Over the last 180 days, Aave Labs shipped a myriad of UI and UX improvements to Aave Pro on mobile and web.

The new markets page in Aave Pro brings each V4 market’s data, deposit and borrow assets, connected Hubs, and composition into a single view, and new reserve pages show each asset’s interest rates, supply and borrow caps, and top addresses. Watch wallets lets users track the V4 positions, balances, and activity of any wallet without connecting it, with custom names and avatars, and Merkl rewards lets users track and claim incentive rewards from Merkl, a rewards distribution platform, without leaving Aave Pro. With Avalanche support and the additions of Arc and Base, Aave Pro now covers every DAO-operated V4 deployment.

Aave Labs’ backend and full-stack engineers also rebuilt the system that indexes Aave V4 and serves its data to the Aave API and Aave Pro. The new backend consolidates protocol data into a single pipeline that is more robust, faster, and cheaper to run, and initial estimates show a 50x improvement on some of the heaviest load times in Aave Pro. Aave Labs started with V4 and will begin moving every protocol version and other data sources onto the same pipeline, which will let the team ship new features faster and give integrators confidence that the data they display is accurate.

The Earn and Borrow flows in Aave Pro were also rebuilt in Q3, which give users a clearer path to deposit, earn, and borrow across Aave V4 markets, and the new Earn flow replaced the Deposit page in October. The team also spent Q3 working on the functionality behind position swaps, which let users swap their collateral or debt from one asset to another without unwinding and reopening the position. Position swaps are expected to launch in Q4. Aave Labs is also developing a leverage feature for Aave Pro, which would let users open a leveraged position in a single flow instead of looping deposits and borrows by hand, and it is also expected to launch in Q4.

Aave V3 Interface

In July, the Staked GHO to Savings GHO migration tool went live so that stkGHO holders could move into Savings GHO in one step and keep earning at the Aave Savings Rate. In September, Aave Labs released a full redesign of the Aave V3 interface to bring the UI/UX to a standard expected from Aave products. This was followed by asset swaps and position swaps powered by CoW Swap on the Plasma market, which let users swap any asset, or swap their collateral and debt, with protection against front-running.

Aave Kit

Stable Vaults launched in July as the vault infrastructure behind Aave App, with per-user earning rates, earning across multiple chains and strategies, and deposits and withdrawals in multiple stablecoins. Any business can use Stable Vaults to embed onchain stablecoin yield in its own product, choosing which stablecoins to accept, which strategies to run, and what rate to offer each user, without building the underlying infrastructure itself. Certora formally verified the Stable Vault, Funds Handler, Asset Registry, Allocator, and IOU token contracts.

Aave Labs released the official Aave MCP server in September. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is the standard AI assistants use to connect to outside tools, and the Aave MCP server gives those assistants one endpoint to read protocol data, manage positions, and prepare transactions across every Aave V3 and V4 deployment, with no authentication, API key, or signup required. The server never holds user funds and returns unsigned transactions for the user’s own wallet to approve.

Aave Labs’ design engineering team developed the refraction technique behind Aave Glass for the web, along with the family of interface components that use it. The technique works in Chromium, Safari, and Firefox on desktop and mobile, and Aave Labs published a write-up that covers the displacement map, the WebGL path for canvas and video surfaces, and other implementation details.

Aave Institutional

Aave Labs spent Q2 and Q3 building out new institutional pipelines including a new credit offering designed to bring institutional users to Aave, and brought the Aave Institutional ARFC to Snapshot on September 30. A governance proposal published on September 15 also introduced Custodied Collateral Lending on V4, which would let institutions borrow stablecoins against assets held in custody at Anchorage, with balances kept in sync onchain through Chainlink CustodySync. Together, these initiatives are intended to open Aave to institutional users it has not previously reached.

In June, Bitwise became the investment manager of USCC on Aave Horizon, which already held over $120 million USCC deposits, and Midas’s mGLOBAL went live on June 23 with a strategy managed by Fasanara Capital. Active loans backed by real-world assets on Aave Horizon and other Aave markets passed $500 million on June 30.

Securitize also proposed onboarding HINC, the Neuberger Securitize High Income Tokenized Fund, to Aave Horizon, and Midas proposed onboarding mWIN, a fixed income strategy managed by Wellington Management. In September, Aave Labs also announced V4’s first RWA Hub on Avalanche, which is expected to use Tether’s USA₮ as its main source of dollar liquidity, and work on the Hub is underway ahead of launch.

Security and Infrastructure

Throughout Q2 and Q3, Aave Labs built out a dedicated smart contract security team, which now sits under the new Chief Information Security Officer role, and scoped, scheduled, and managed more than 20 security engagements across the protocol and product stack.

On April 10, Aave Labs completed a SOC 2 Type II examination covering the Trust Services Criteria of Security, Availability, and Confidentiality, an independent assessment of the controls Aave Labs uses to develop and operate its software.

The bug bounty restructure went live on May 14, which aligned payouts with the risk level of each part of the Aave ecosystem, simplified the review process, and raised the payout caps for critical bugs fivefold on Aave V4 and Core Aave V3. Aave’s bug bounties now run on Immunefi, Sherlock, and Cantina, with ongoing triage of submitted reports.

On August 13, Aave Labs published the first results from AI-assisted security scanning of V3 and V4, which adds automated review alongside the human audits that have covered every Aave protocol generation since 2020.

Aave Labs also published the Technical Asset Listing Framework on May 28, which sets one technical standard for every new asset listing, continued listing, and material parameter change across Aave V3, Aave V4, and Aave Horizon.

Aave Labs also supported LlamaRisk’s initiative to derisk low-value assets on Aave V3 by implementing the payloads for AIP 521, which deprecated low-adoption assets, and AIP 526, which deprecated the oracles for long-tail assets.

Throughout Q2-Q3, Aave Labs published technical network assessments ahead of each new deployment. Aave Labs also implemented the payload that funded Certora’s Concord Equivalence Checker, a tool that confirms upgraded contracts behave the same as the code they replace, and in August it led the rotation of signers on the Aave Governance Emergency Guardian, the multisig that can cancel malicious governance proposals.

Aave Labs also supported the setup of emergency multisigs for V4 and Aave Horizon, strengthened device and identity security across the team in response to industry-wide phishing activity, ran disaster recovery and key-holder readiness exercises, and published a new security page at aave.com/security.

Summary

Over the last 180 days, Aave Labs’ team of about 97 team members put an estimated 100,000 hours into its work for the Aave DAO and completed 6,096 tracked issues and 36 projects of various scopes across engineering, security, product, design, growth, marketing, governance, and legal. Over the same period, Aave Labs authored 26 onchain governance proposals and 20 Snapshot votes, and shipped 28 items including products, features, and protocol deployments. Aave Labs also prepared and implemented the DAO-approved onboarding of 33 unique assets, deployments on four new chains, and four new Aave V4 Liquidity Hubs with their corresponding Spokes.

Throughout Q2, Aave Labs assumed roughly 40 technical and supporting functions that BGD Labs and the Aave Chan Initiative (ACI) previously performed for the DAO, including contract maintenance, security coordination, proposal payload engineering, and developer tooling, and it completed both transitions while rsETH incident response (detailed below) was still underway.

Q3 was a strong quarter for launches and product expansion across the Aave ecosystem. Following DAO approval, Aave Labs implemented Aave V4 deployments on Avalanche, Arc, and Base, and V4 grew from $212.6 million deposits to $1.34 billion in Q3, passing its first $1 billion on September 16. Since launching from zero at the end of March, V4 has grown to more than $1.3 billion deposits in roughly six months. Aave App opened early access on iOS, expanded to five total chains, and launched instant onramps for eligible U.S. users through licensed third-party providers. We also opened up Stable Vaults, the vault infrastructure behind the Aave App, for enterprise use. Other key launches include the official Aave MCP server, which gives AI a direct connection to read Aave data and prepare transactions, the Aave V3 interface redesign, and the addition of each new V4 deployment to Aave Pro.

On the security side, Certora completed formal verification of core Aave V4 and Stable Vaults contracts against defined specifications, and three new V4 security audits were published over the period. rsETH Response

On April 18 at 17:35 UTC, an exploit of the rsETH cross-chain bridge resulted in the release of 116,500 rsETH on Ethereum without a matching amount being burned on the source chain. The exploit did not involve the Aave Protocol’s smart contracts, which continued to operate as designed. The attacker supplied 89,567 of the stolen rsETH across eight Aave V3 positions and borrowed 82,650 WETH and 821 wstETH against it, after which the Aave Protocol Guardian froze the affected reserves within 85 minutes and the Risk Stewards made roughly 295 parameter changes across V3 reserves over the following weeks to contain exposure.

Aave Labs, TokenLogic, and LlamaRisk then helped coordinate DeFi United, a cross-protocol effort to restore rsETH’s backing for affected users. Within a week, Consensys and Joseph Lubin committed up to 30,000 ETH with strategic advice from SharpLink, Aave service providers proposed that Aave DAO contribute 25,000 ETH, and Golem contributed 1,000 ETH, while EtherFi, Ethena, Mantle, Frax, the Ink Foundation, Tydro, and LayerZero also joined the effort.

On April 25, Aave service providers, together with EtherFi, Kelp, LayerZero, Compound, and others, submitted a proposal asking the Arbitrum DAO to release into the recovery the ETH that the Arbitrum Security Council had frozen after the exploit. The vote reached quorum with more than 1,600 addresses representing over 190 million ARB. On May 1, a restraining notice was issued against the Arbitrum DAO in connection with an unrelated case. Following an application by Aave LLC, the court modified the notice on May 8 to allow the onchain vote and the transfer of the ETH to Aave LLC.

Aave governance executed AIP 478 on May 6, which liquidated the eight attacker positions without affecting any other users or Umbrella, Aave’s staking-based backstop. AIP 482 followed on May 16 and restored WETH borrowing limits to their pre-incident levels across the V3 Ethereum Core, Ethereum Prime, Arbitrum, Base, Mantle, and Linea markets. Kelp refilled the bridge with recovered rsETH across five tranches totaling 116,131.72 rsETH, which fully restored rsETH’s backing by May 26 and returned all Aave markets to normal operation.

Aave Labs prioritized its incident response work over its launch schedule and moved the affected launches into Q3. The public post mortem gives a fuller account of the response.

Aave Labs authored 26 onchain proposals and 20 Snapshot votes over the 180 days, and it submitted another 16 onchain proposals on behalf of other service providers. Onchain proposals are binding votes that execute code on the protocol, and Snapshot votes are offchain votes the DAO uses to approve a direction before the onchain step.

Aave Labs submitted the other 16 proposals in collaboration with TokenLogic, LlamaRisk, Chaos Labs, and Certora as part of the payload engineering function it took over from BGD Labs. A payload is the smart contract code that a proposal executes, and Aave Labs now writes, tests, and submits that code for other service providers in addition to its own proposals.

Aave Labs also published the Technical Asset Listing Framework to the governance forum on May 28, which sets one technical standard for every new asset listing, continued listing, and material parameter expansion across Aave V3, Aave V4, and Aave Horizon, along with requirements for ongoing monitoring of listed assets. The framework passed Snapshot in July and is now a formal part of the asset onboarding process.

Aave Labs is also adapting the Correlated Assets Price Oracle (CAPO) to V4. CAPO limits how quickly the price of a yield-bearing asset such as wstETH can rise, which protects Aave markets from price manipulation.

Through the same transition, Aave Labs took on security coordination and vulnerability response support for V3 and earlier versions, along with ongoing contract maintenance for those versions and the deprecation of the legacy Safety Module. V4-Specific Security and Risk Management

Aave Labs’ smart contract security team led the security work on V4 over the 180 days. Alongside external audits, the team introduced AI-assisted code review across Aave Labs repositories and coordinated each external engagement through scoping, remediation, and fix review.

Aave Labs worked with Certora to formally verify the core V4 contracts in July, covering the Liquidity Hub, the Spoke, and the Tokenization Spoke contracts along with the math libraries they rely on. Aave Labs also worked with Sherlock on a new V4 security audit published May 26, and with ChainSecurity on two more, one on the Tokenization Spoke published June 19 and one on the Liquidity Hub, Spoke, and position manager contracts published July 21.

Aave Labs also worked to integrate Chainlink SVR into Aave V4 markets for eligible assets. SVR, short for Smart Value Recapture, captures the profit that bots earn from liquidations and returns it to the DAO, and on V3 it has returned over $11 million to the DAO treasury since March 2025.

Product Overview

Over the 180 days covered in this report, Aave product surface area expanded significantly, including a consumer app for earning onchain stablecoin yield, enterprise vault infrastructure, a direct connection for AI agents, and a redesigned V3 app. Aave Labs shipped several items including products, features, and protocol deployments over the 180 days.

Aave App

Aave App opened to its first users through Ghost Passes on August 26, and since then users from around the world have started using the app, funding it with stablecoins or from their bank accounts through Push and licensed providers. Balances across all Aave App users have since crossed $45 million.

During Q3, Aave Labs added instant deposit onboarding for eligible U.S. users, provided through licensed providers, and expanded Aave App from one chain to five, adding Ethereum, Base, HyperEVM, and BNB Chain to Arbitrum so users can deposit stablecoins from any of those networks. Aave Labs also spent Q3 developing the Android version of the app, which we currently expect to complete in the coming months.

During the period, Aave Labs’ UK subsidiaries Push Labs Limited and Push Virtual Assets Limited were registered with the Financial Conduct Authority as cryptoasset exchange providers under the Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017.

Aave Pro

Over the last 180 days, Aave Labs shipped a myriad of UI and UX improvements to Aave Pro on mobile and web.

The new markets page in Aave Pro brings each V4 market’s data, deposit and borrow assets, connected Hubs, and composition into a single view, and new reserve pages show each asset’s interest rates, supply and borrow caps, and top addresses. Watch wallets lets users track the V4 positions, balances, and activity of any wallet without connecting it, with custom names and avatars, and Merkl rewards lets users track and claim incentive rewards from Merkl, a rewards distribution platform, without leaving Aave Pro. With Avalanche support and the additions of Arc and Base, Aave Pro now covers every DAO-operated V4 deployment.

Aave Labs’ backend and full-stack engineers also rebuilt the system that indexes Aave V4 and serves its data to the Aave API and Aave Pro. The new backend consolidates protocol data into a single pipeline that is more robust, faster, and cheaper to run, and initial estimates show a 50x improvement on some of the heaviest load times in Aave Pro. Aave Labs started with V4 and will begin moving every protocol version and other data sources onto the same pipeline, which will let the team ship new features faster and give integrators confidence that the data they display is accurate.

The Earn and Borrow flows in Aave Pro were also rebuilt in Q3, which give users a clearer path to deposit, earn, and borrow across Aave V4 markets, and the new Earn flow replaced the Deposit page in October. The team also spent Q3 working on the functionality behind position swaps, which let users swap their collateral or debt from one asset to another without unwinding and reopening the position. Position swaps are expected to launch in Q4. Aave Labs is also developing a leverage feature for Aave Pro, which would let users open a leveraged position in a single flow instead of looping deposits and borrows by hand, and it is also expected to launch in Q4.

Aave V3 Interface

In July, the Staked GHO to Savings GHO migration tool went live so that stkGHO holders could move into Savings GHO in one step and keep earning at the Aave Savings Rate. In September, Aave Labs released a full redesign of the Aave V3 interface to bring the UI/UX to a standard expected from Aave products. This was followed by asset swaps and position swaps powered by CoW Swap on the Plasma market, which let users swap any asset, or swap their collateral and debt, with protection against front-running.

Aave Kit

Stable Vaults launched in July as the vault infrastructure behind Aave App, with per-user earning rates, earning across multiple chains and strategies, and deposits and withdrawals in multiple stablecoins. Any business can use Stable Vaults to embed onchain stablecoin yield in its own product, choosing which stablecoins to accept, which strategies to run, and what rate to offer each user, without building the underlying infrastructure itself. Certora formally verified the Stable Vault, Funds Handler, Asset Registry, Allocator, and IOU token contracts.

Aave Labs released the official Aave MCP server in September. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is the standard AI assistants use to connect to outside tools, and the Aave MCP server gives those assistants one endpoint to read protocol data, manage positions, and prepare transactions across every Aave V3 and V4 deployment, with no authentication, API key, or signup required. The server never holds user funds and returns unsigned transactions for the user’s own wallet to approve.

Aave Labs’ design engineering team developed the refraction technique behind Aave Glass for the web, along with the family of interface components that use it. The technique works in Chromium, Safari, and Firefox on desktop and mobile, and Aave Labs published a write-up that covers the displacement map, the WebGL path for canvas and video surfaces, and other implementation details.

Aave Institutional

Aave Labs spent Q2 and Q3 building out new institutional pipelines including a new credit offering designed to bring institutional users to Aave, and brought the Aave Institutional ARFC to Snapshot on September 30. A governance proposal published on September 15 also introduced Custodied Collateral Lending on V4, which would let institutions borrow stablecoins against assets held in custody at Anchorage, with balances kept in sync onchain through Chainlink CustodySync. Together, these initiatives are intended to open Aave to institutional users it has not previously reached.

In June, Bitwise became the investment manager of USCC on Aave Horizon, which already held over $120 million USCC deposits, and Midas’s mGLOBAL went live on June 23 with a strategy managed by Fasanara Capital. Active loans backed by real-world assets on Aave Horizon and other Aave markets passed $500 million on June 30.

Securitize also proposed onboarding HINC, the Neuberger Securitize High Income Tokenized Fund, to Aave Horizon, and Midas proposed onboarding mWIN, a fixed income strategy managed by Wellington Management. In September, Aave Labs also announced V4’s first RWA Hub on Avalanche, which is expected to use Tether’s USA₮ as its main source of dollar liquidity, and work on the Hub is underway ahead of launch.

Security and Infrastructure

Throughout Q2 and Q3, Aave Labs built out a dedicated smart contract security team, which now sits under the new Chief Information Security Officer role, and scoped, scheduled, and managed more than 20 security engagements across the protocol and product stack.

On April 10, Aave Labs completed a SOC 2 Type II examination covering the Trust Services Criteria of Security, Availability, and Confidentiality, an independent assessment of the controls Aave Labs uses to develop and operate its software.

The bug bounty restructure went live on May 14, which aligned payouts with the risk level of each part of the Aave ecosystem, simplified the review process, and raised the payout caps for critical bugs fivefold on Aave V4 and Core Aave V3. Aave’s bug bounties now run on Immunefi, Sherlock, and Cantina, with ongoing triage of submitted reports.

On August 13, Aave Labs published the first results from AI-assisted security scanning of V3 and V4, which adds automated review alongside the human audits that have covered every Aave protocol generation since 2020.

Aave Labs also published the Technical Asset Listing Framework on May 28, which sets one technical standard for every new asset listing, continued listing, and material parameter change across Aave V3, Aave V4, and Aave Horizon.

Aave Labs also supported LlamaRisk’s initiative to derisk low-value assets on Aave V3 by implementing the payloads for AIP 521, which deprecated low-adoption assets, and AIP 526, which deprecated the oracles for long-tail assets.

Throughout Q2-Q3, Aave Labs published technical network assessments ahead of each new deployment. Aave Labs also implemented the payload that funded Certora’s Concord Equivalence Checker, a tool that confirms upgraded contracts behave the same as the code they replace, and in August it led the rotation of signers on the Aave Governance Emergency Guardian, the multisig that can cancel malicious governance proposals.

Aave Labs also supported the setup of emergency multisigs for V4 and Aave Horizon, strengthened device and identity security across the team in response to industry-wide phishing activity, ran disaster recovery and key-holder readiness exercises, and published a new security page at aave.com/security.

title: [Direct-to-AIP] Asset Listing - USDC Plasma
author: @TokenLogic
created: 2026-11-18

Summary

This proposal seeks to onboard native USDC as a supported asset on the Aave V3 Plasma Instance.

Circle deployed USDC natively on Plasma on August 28, 2026, alongside EURC, the Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol, and Bridge Kit. This proposal expands the stablecoin offering on Aave V3 Plasma and gives users an additional highly liquid, fiat-backed asset for supplying, borrowing, and collateral use, configured in line with USDT0.

Motivation

On August 28, 2026, Circle announced native USDC on Plasma, along with institutional on and off ramps through Circle Mint. Circle issues native USDC on Plasma, fully reserved and redeemable 1:1 for US dollars through eligible Circle channels. CCTP enables native USDC to be transferred between Plasma and other supported networks without relying on wrapped or third-party bridged representations.

Aave V3 Plasma is today a USDT0-centric market. USDT0 is the only fiat-backed stablecoin listed and carries roughly $603M of supply against $552M of borrows (about 92% utilisation), with USDe and GHO as the other borrowable stablecoins. Every stablecoin-borrowing eMode category on the instance points to USDT0.

Onboarding USDC to Aave V3 Plasma would:

  • Add a second fiat-backed stablecoin to the instance, reducing single-issuer concentration on the stablecoin side of the book.
  • Provide an additional asset for lending and borrowing alongside USDT0, USDe, and GHO.
  • Increase the stablecoin borrowing liquidity available to the existing USDe, sUSDe, weETH, syrupUSDT, WXPL, GHO and PT-sUSDe eMode categories.
  • Enable users and institutions to access native USDC liquidity supported by Circle Mint and CCTP infrastructure, and to move USDC between Plasma and other Aave deployments (Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Avalanche, X Layer) via CCTP.

Plasma is a stablecoin-focused network, and the arrival of Circle’s native issuance gives Aave V3 Plasma direct access to the second largest stablecoin without bridge dependencies.

Specification

USDC Contract Address

Asset Address
USDC 0x2d661C89D812261039AF9764eceaAee884f5F67F

The address above represents Circle-issued native USDC on Plasma (6 decimals), as published in Circle’s contract address reference.

Proposed Market Configuration

We propose configuring USDC in line with the parameters currently applied to USDT0 on Aave V3 Plasma, consistent with the approach LlamaRisk recommended for the recent USDC listing on X Layer (USDC aligned to the local USDT0 risk parameters, 75% LTV and 78% LT, with a CAPO stable adapter). Supply and borrow caps mirror the X Layer listing and can be raised through the Risk Steward as USDC liquidity on Plasma develops. Final parameters remain subject to Risk Service Provider recommendations.

Final onboarding parameters remain subject to review and recommendations from Aave’s Risk Service Providers.

Liquidity

Native USDC on Plasma is only days old: roughly 4.5M USDC has been minted at the time of writing, and on-chain DEX liquidity is still nascent. As with the X Layer listing, liquidity is expected to build as supply flows to the chain through CCTP and Circle Mint, and the proposed caps leave room for Risk Service Providers to sequence activation or adjust caps based on observed liquidity at execution.

eMode Configuration

We propose adding USDC as a borrowable asset to the eight current-generation eMode categories on Plasma in which USDT0 is borrowable today. This proposal does not modify the collateral, LTV, LT, or Liquidation Bonus parameters for any category; it only adds USDC as a borrowable asset to each mentioned eMode.

Oracle

A Chainlink USDC/USD Price Feed is already available on Plasma Mainnet.

Chainlink identifies this feed as USDC/USD-RefPrice-DF-Plasma-001.

We propose pricing USDC through the Chainlink USDC/USD feed wrapped in a CAPO stable adapter (PriceCapAdapterStable) with the upward price deviation capped at 4% ($1.04), in line with LlamaRisk’s recommendation for USDC on X Layer and identical to the cap of the Capped USDT/USD adapter (0xdBbB0b5DD13E7AC9C56624834ef193df87b022c3) currently used for USDT0 on Plasma. The final oracle configuration is to be confirmed by the relevant Aave Risk and Technical Service Providers.

Disclaimer

TokenLogic is an active service provider to the Aave DAO, the beneficiary of stream 100086 and the KPI as outlined in this publication. The scope of this engagement is available via this forum proposal.

TokenLogic supports and maintains an independent delegate voting platform within the Aave community.

TokenLogic and associated entities have no undisclosed material conflicts of interest at the time of submission.

Next Steps

  1. Gather feedback from the community.
  2. Using the Direct-to-AIP process, incorporate feedback from the Risk Service Provider.
  3. Escalate this proposal to the AIP Voting stage.

The forecast weights the stock’s recent moves and pulls them partly toward the market-wide level. The collateral factor is what remains after the haircut, the maximum liquidation bonus and an allowance for interest while a position waits for liquidation, rounded down to a whole point and capped at 65%, which binds on NFLXc. Each of the six feeds is expected to meet these requirements, as MSTRc’s live feed does:

  • It prices the token as the underlying share price times the issuer multiplier, as on the listed reserves.
  • It publishes through the pre-market, regular, post-market and overnight sessions, from Sunday 20:00 to Friday 20:00 ET.
  • It updates on a deviation threshold of at most 0.5%, the oracle allowance in the collateral factor, and a heartbeat of at most 24 hours within those sessions.

The feeds stop updating from Friday 20:00 to Sunday 20:00 ET and on US market holidays, and keep showing the last price. Positions can still be liquidated in that window, but only at that price, so a move in the stock over the weekend reaches positions when the feed restarts on Sunday evening.

3. Perpetual Futures

Perpetual futures let a liquidator hedge seized collateral while the cash market is closed. All six names trade on Binance, Hyperliquid, and OKX, and all except NFLX on Lighter. Open interest is counted once per contract on every venue, so Hyperliquid’s reported figure, which sums long and short positions, is halved.

Turnover relative to open interest is highest on AMD, at about 10.5 times its open interest in a day.

Perpetual markets on MSTR, AMD and ORCL are deep enough to hedge a large liquidation. A quarter of a full USD 5M cap is about 1.1% of MSTR’s open interest. On PLTR, NFLX and NOW they are thinner, so a hedge of a quarter of a full cap, USD 1.25M, would move their price, especially at weekends. The hedge is not needed to protect the market: the collateral factor covers the fall until the next regular session, when seized tokens can be redeemed or sold, and the cap limits the amount at risk to USD 5M per token.


Source: Binance, Hyperliquid, OKX and Lighter, November 11, 2026

Over the last 30 days, median weekday volume across the four venues ranged from USD 3.3M (NOW) to USD 345.9M (MSTR), with weekend volume at a ninth to about a fifth of weekday levels. Open interest on Binance and OKX roughly halved on PLTR (USD 16.7M to 8.9M), eased on ORCL (USD 25.7M to 17.6M), held steady on NFLX (USD 7.0M to 6.9M), and ended level on AMD (USD 29.1M to 28.3M) after a peak of USD 56.2M around its results. Each token is a CB Certificate issued by Coinbase Onchain SPV Ltd under a series prospectus approved by the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Abu Dhabi Global Market between September 3 and October 7, 2026 (NFLXc, ORCLc, PLTRc, AMDc, NOWc, MSTRc). Apart from the series details, the description of the underlying issuer, and minor drafting changes, the NFLXc, ORCLc, PLTRc, AMDc and NOWc prospectuses carry the text of the SpaceX prospectus of September 3, 2026, whose terms and conditions and deed of trust are those of the NVIDIA series examined in the technical review and the SPCXc assessment. The MSTRc prospectus, approved the same day as SpaceX’s, differs from it in the series details only. The tokens use the same B20 standard and Token Supply Manager as the listed reserves, and their admin, operator, pause, metadata, mint, and burn roles are held by the same addresses as on the listed Coinbase tokens.

Anyone who acquires the tokens on the secondary market, a liquidator included, holds them as an unvested holder, with no redemption right until it completes the issuer’s vesting process. The issuer’s operator can change a token’s multiplier by any amount in one transaction, and the feed carries the new value into the price at its next update. Announced corporate actions run with the issuer’s registry pause, during which the feed holds its last value and minting and redemption stop. 5.1 Collateral Factor

In Aave V4 the collateral factor is both the borrowing limit and the liquidation threshold. For a stock priced 24/5, it has to cover the largest fall from any off-hours price to the lowest price before five minutes past the next regular open, plus a 0.5% allowance for the feed’s deviation threshold. It is sized so that this fall exceeds a stock’s haircut on one night per stock in ten years, with a 2020-type crash counted as one year in ten.

The haircut scales a forecast of the stock’s daily volatility over the next year by the size of a once-in-ten-years off-hours fall relative to daily volatility, measured across S&P 500 stocks. The forecast weights the stock’s recent moves and pulls them partly toward the market-wide level. governance_posts.title: Aave DeFi Watcher – Browser Extension for Monitoring Aave Positions
governance_posts.description:
Hi dear aave community :)

I’d like to share Aave DeFi Watcher, a browser extension I built to make monitoring Aave positions simple, fast, and privacy-friendly.

I originally started building it because the previously shared Aave Monitor extension appears to no longer function reliably. For example, many addresses currently return “Failed to fetch” instead of account data. It also only supports Aave V3, while I wanted a tool that could monitor positions across Aave V2, V3, and V4. Since I needed a working solution myself, I decided to build one from scratch.

Features

  • Total Collateral
  • Total Debt
  • Available to Borrow
  • Loan-to-Value (LTV)
  • Liquidation Threshold
  • Health Factor
  • Monitor multiple wallet addresses
  • Support for Aave V2, V3, and V4
  • Support for multiple networks including Ethereum, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, Polygon, and Avalanche
  • Desktop notifications for Health Factor alerts
  • Privacy Mode to hide balances while continuing to monitor your positions
  • Automatic RPC fallback for improved reliability

One of my favorite features is the extension badge, which displays the Health Factor of your selected address directly on the browser toolbar, allowing you to monitor your position at a glance.

The extension is completely read-only. It never asks you to connect a wallet or sign transactions. All account data is fetched directly from Aave’s public smart contracts.

Chrome Web Store

chromewebstore.google.com

Aave DeFi Watcher - Chrome Web Store

Monitor your Aave health factor and liquidation risk in real time across chains.

I built this extension for my own daily use and decided to share it with the community. It’s actively maintained, and I plan to continue adding new features and supporting future Aave releases.

I’d really appreciate any feedback, bug reports or feature suggestions from the community :))

title: [Research] Targeted Deleveraging of rsETH and osETH Through Exchange Rate Growth Discounting

author: @TokenLogic

created: 2026-11-24

Summary

LlamaRisk’s ARFC: Repositioning Aave V3 Core Around Established & Liquid Collateral proposes a WETH borrow rate increase as the final follow up control for the rsETH and osETH loops, should voluntary migration and natural unwinding prove insufficient.

This analysis proposes a more targeted alternative before resorting to a WETH borrow rate increase: setting maxYearlyRatioGrowthPercent to 0% on the rsETH and osETH CAPO adapters. Unlike a WETH borrow rate increase, this approach does not impose additional borrowing costs across the entire WETH reserve.

For rsETH, the unwinding timeline can be accelerated further through sized E-Mode liquidation threshold reductions, following an initial borrower engagement and migration window. This provides a more targeted path to reducing exposure while preserving the migration route proposed in LlamaRisk’s ARFC.

Motivation

A WETH borrow rate increase applies to the entire WETH reserve, affecting every ETH loop on Core, including wstETH and weETH positions that the ARFC intends to retain. This means increasing borrowing costs across approximately $3.4B of WETH debt to address approximately $860M of rsETH and osETH loop exposure.

Merkl rebates can partially offset the additional borrowing costs, but do not eliminate the associated friction. Interest accrues continuously, while borrowers must manually claim rebates, stake them, and resupply before recovering their health factors. This creates an ongoing operational burden for borrowers, risks driving existing users to competing lending markets, and incurs additional fees for the DAO to run the Merkl campaigns.

Exchange Rate Growth Discounting Through CAPO

LST/LRT oracles on Aave combine three components:

  1. The ETH/USD price feed.
  2. The underlying protocol’s exchange rate.
  3. A CAPO adapter, which caps the exchange rate at a maximum value.

The CAPO adapter returns the lower of the live exchange rate and a maximum rate that grows at maxYearlyRatioGrowthPercent from a snapshot:

CAPO was designed to protect against upward manipulation of exchange rates. However, the same mechanism can also be used to limit the exchange rate appreciation recognized by Aave for specific collateral assets.

Setting maxYearlyRatioGrowthPercent to 0% effectively freezes the maximum permitted exchange rate at its initial snapshot. As the underlying asset continues to accrue staking yields any appreciation beyond this cap is no longer reflected in its collateral valuation on Aave. This does not change the underlying exchange rate or the asset’s actual redemption value; it only limits the value recognized by Aave’s oracle.

For leveraged positions, this creates a gradual deterioration in health factors: the collateral no longer benefits from exchange rate appreciation, while the WETH debt continues to accrue interest. Borrowers must progressively reduce leverage to maintain their health factors, making these loops increasingly unattractive and incentivizing an orderly unwind.

Each asset has its own CAPO adapter, allowing rsETH and osETH to be targeted independently without affecting other collateral assets or their respective ETH loops.

Projected Impact

The underlying exchange rates of rsETH and osETH currently grow at approximately 2.4% and 2.2% per year, respectively. Setting maxYearlyRatioGrowthPercent to 0% removes this appreciation from Aave’s collateral valuation. Meanwhile, WETH debt continues to accrue interest, progressively reducing the health factors of leveraged positions.

Assuming no borrower intervention and a constant WETH borrow rate, the time for a position to reach HF below 1 can be approximated as:

where (HF_0) is the initial health factor and (r) is the annualized WETH borrow rate.

Based on onchain positions as of 13 November 2026, the following table shows the cumulative collateral value of positions projected to reach HF below 1 under this scenario:

The projections show that CAPO adjustments alone can create meaningful deleveraging pressure, but the impact is relatively slow for rsETH. While osETH exposure is largely brought to liquidation within 18 months, the first material rsETH liquidations occur around month 6, with most of the exposure remaining beyond month 18.

This makes CAPO adjustments an effective mechanism for establishing a predictable exit timeline, but insufficient on their own to accelerate the rsETH unwind. The timeline can be shortened considerably by combining the CAPO adjustment with a series of carefully sized E-Mode liquidation threshold reductions, as discussed in the following section.

Accelerating the rsETH Unwind with E-Mode LT Reductions

rsETH loops sit in a dedicated E Mode category (“rsETH / ETH, wstETH, ETHx”), allowing their liquidation timeline to be shortened through targeted LT reductions without affecting other ETH loops on Core.

Rather than applying a single substantial LT reduction, the proposed approach uses a series of smaller adjustments, each calibrated against the health factors of remaining positions. This brings liquidation events forward incrementally while ensuring that no position becomes liquidatable immediately upon execution.

The process would follow a recurring cycle:

  1. Set the rsETH CAPO maxYearlyRatioGrowthPercent to 0%.
  2. Engagement window. Borrowers have time to unwind or migrate voluntarily.
  3. Assess the tightest remaining position. If it would reach HF < 1 within one month, make no change. Otherwise, reduce the E-Mode LT just enough to bring its projected liquidation to one month away.
  4. Wait for the liquidation and repeat Step 3 until no rsETH loops remain.

The first LT reduction is applied at the start of the cycle, once the engagement and migration window has closed. Its magnitude is determined by the health factors of the remaining positions at that point. Based on current positions, a reduction from 95% to 94.18% would bring the first projected liquidation forward from month 6 to month 1. However, as health factors continue to deteriorate under the 0% CAPO growth cap during the engagement window, the reduction required at the start of the cycle is expected to be smaller.

Following each liquidation episode, the next LT reduction is calibrated against the remaining positions using the same approach, bringing the next projected liquidation to one month ahead.

This approach ensures that each adjustment provides at least one month of notice before the next projected liquidation event. The interval can also be extended to accommodate available onchain liquidity and the beacon chain withdrawal queue.

Assuming passive borrowers, this iterative approach brings approximately 48% of rsETH collateral to liquidation within 12 months and approximately 72% within 24 months, compared with approximately 3% and 33%, respectively, under the CAPO adjustment alone.

Interaction with the ARFC’s migration path

The ARFC proposes adding wstETH, weETH and cbETH as collateral to the existing rsETH E Mode category, allowing borrowers to migrate their collateral without first repaying their WETH debt. We support this approach, as it provides borrowers with a straightforward migration path and facilitates the voluntary reduction of rsETH exposure.

However, subsequent E-Mode LT reductions would also affect positions that have already migrated to these assets, potentially penalizing borrowers who followed the proposed migration path. This needs to be addressed through appropriate sequencing of the migration and LT reduction processes.

This can be avoided by sequencing the migration and LT reduction processes:

  1. Migration window: Give rsETH borrowers time to swap their collateral into wstETH, weETH or cbETH within the rsETH E Mode category, as proposed in the ARFC.
  2. Move migrated positions to the standard ETH-correlated E Mode: Once migrated, borrowers can switch to the existing ETH-correlated E Mode, which has the same 93% / 95% LT / LTV parameters and WETH as a borrowable asset. This transition has no impact on their health factors.
  3. Begin the LT reduction cycle: Announce a fixed start date for the first LT reduction. By that point, the rsETH E-Mode category should contain only remaining rsETH positions, allowing subsequent LT reductions to target the intended exposure without affecting migrated borrowers.

This sequencing preserves the ARFC’s migration route while allowing the remaining rsETH loops to follow a shorter and more predictable unwinding timeline.

The DAO as Liquidator of Last Resort

In a worst case scenario with limited voluntary unwinding, the debt liquidated during these episodes may exceed available secondary market liquidity.

The DAO should therefore be prepared to fund these liquidations using treasury ETH and exit the seized rsETH through Kelp’s withdrawal queue.

Depending on the expected liquidation volume, the E-Mode liquidation bonus could also be increased ahead of each episode to compensate the DAO for the additional duration risk associated with holding seized rsETH until it can be redeemed through the withdrawal queue.

osETH Considerations

osETH shares the ETH correlated E-Mode with wstETH, weETH and cbETH. Therefore, E-Mode LT reductions cannot selectively target osETH positions without affecting other ETH loops. Setting maxYearlyRatioGrowthPercent to 0% on the osETH CAPO adapter remains the only targeted mechanism.

Overall Assessment

  • Targeted: CAPO adjustments affect only rsETH and osETH collateral valuations, leaving WETH borrowing costs and other ETH loops unchanged.
  • Predictable: The mechanism provides borrowers with time to unwind voluntarily, with liquidation timelines determined by individual position health factors.
  • Gradual: Borrowers can continue benefiting from the underlying exchange rate appreciation, but must progressively reduce leverage to maintain healthy positions.
  • Controlled market impact: Liquidations are distributed over time and occur partially, subject to the 50% close factor.
  • Accelerated rsETH unwind: E Mode LT reductions provide an additional mechanism to bring liquidation timelines forward without affecting other ETH loops, provided migrated positions are moved to the standard ETH correlated E Mode first.
  • Implementation: No new contracts or development are required. The analysis relies on updates to existing CAPO parameters and E Mode configuration.
  • Limitations: The rsETH CAPO adapter is currently shared across Aave V3 Core, V3 Prime and the V4 Kelp spoke. Should the CAPO adjustment be pursued, it could be scoped to the intended V3 markets by deploying a dedicated rsETH CAPO adapter and updating the corresponding oracle source, leaving other deployments that use the existing adapter unchanged. The treatment of other deployments is outside the scope of this analysis.

Conclusion and Potential Implementation Path

The following sequence combines the initial measures and migration path proposed in LlamaRisk’s ARFC with the targeted deleveraging mechanisms outlined in this analysis:

  1. Implement initial measures: Freeze osETH and set its LTV to 0%. rsETH is already frozen. Retain the ARFC’s proposed E-Mode additions to facilitate collateral migration.
  2. Apply CAPO adjustments: Set maxYearlyRatioGrowthPercent to 0% on the rsETH and osETH CAPO adapters.

title: [Research] Targeted Deleveraging of rsETH and osETH Through Exchange Rate Growth Discounting

author: @TokenLogic

created: 2026-11-24

Summary

LlamaRisk’s ARFC: Repositioning Aave V3 Core Around Established & Liquid Collateral proposes a WETH borrow rate increase as the final follow up control for the rsETH and osETH loops, should voluntary migration and natural unwinding prove insufficient.

This analysis proposes a more targeted alternative before resorting to a WETH borrow rate increase: setting maxYearlyRatioGrowthPercent to 0% on the rsETH and osETH CAPO adapters. Unlike a WETH borrow rate increase, this approach does not impose additional borrowing costs across the entire WETH reserve.

For rsETH, the unwinding timeline can be accelerated further through sized E-Mode liquidation threshold reductions, following an initial borrower engagement and migration window. This provides a more targeted path to reducing exposure while preserving the migration route proposed in LlamaRisk’s ARFC.

Motivation

A WETH borrow rate increase applies to the entire WETH reserve, affecting every ETH loop on Core, including wstETH and weETH positions that the ARFC intends to retain. This means increasing borrowing costs across approximately $3.4B of WETH debt to address approximately $860M of rsETH and osETH loop exposure.

Merkl rebates can partially offset the additional borrowing costs, but do not eliminate the associated friction. Interest accrues continuously, while borrowers must manually claim rebates, stake them, and resupply before recovering their health factors. This creates an ongoing operational burden for borrowers, risks driving existing users to competing lending markets, and incurs additional fees for the DAO to run the Merkl campaigns.

Exchange Rate Growth Discounting Through CAPO

LST/LRT oracles on Aave combine three components:

  1. The ETH/USD price feed.
  2. The underlying protocol’s exchange rate.
  3. A CAPO adapter, which caps the exchange rate at a maximum value.

The CAPO adapter returns the lower of the live exchange rate and a maximum rate that grows at maxYearlyRatioGrowthPercent from a snapshot:

CAPO was designed to protect against upward manipulation of exchange rates. However, the same mechanism can also be used to limit the exchange rate appreciation recognized by Aave for specific collateral assets.

Setting maxYearlyRatioGrowthPercent to 0% effectively freezes the maximum permitted exchange rate at its initial snapshot. As the underlying asset continues to accrue staking yields any appreciation beyond this cap is no longer reflected in its collateral valuation on Aave. This does not change the underlying exchange rate or the asset’s actual redemption value; it only limits the value recognized by Aave’s oracle.

For leveraged positions, this creates a gradual deterioration in health factors: the collateral no longer benefits from exchange rate appreciation, while the WETH debt continues to accrue interest. Borrowers must progressively reduce leverage to maintain their health factors, making these loops increasingly unattractive and incentivizing an orderly unwind.

Each asset has its own CAPO adapter, allowing rsETH and osETH to be targeted independently without affecting other collateral assets or their respective ETH loops.

Projected Impact

The underlying exchange rates of rsETH and osETH currently grow at approximately 2.4% and 2.2% per year, respectively. Setting maxYearlyRatioGrowthPercent to 0% removes this appreciation from Aave’s collateral valuation. Meanwhile, WETH debt continues to accrue interest, progressively reducing the health factors of leveraged positions.

Assuming no borrower intervention and a constant WETH borrow rate, the time for a position to reach HF below 1 can be approximated as:

where (HF_0) is the initial health factor and (r) is the annualized WETH borrow rate.

Based on onchain positions as of 13 November 2026, the following table shows the cumulative collateral value of positions projected to reach HF below 1 under this scenario:

The projections show that CAPO adjustments alone can create meaningful deleveraging pressure, but the impact is relatively slow for rsETH. While osETH exposure is largely brought to liquidation within 18 months, the first material rsETH liquidations occur around month 6, with most of the exposure remaining beyond month 18.

This makes CAPO adjustments an effective mechanism for establishing a predictable exit timeline, but insufficient on their own to accelerate the rsETH unwind. The timeline can be shortened considerably by combining the CAPO adjustment with a series of carefully sized E-Mode liquidation threshold reductions, as discussed in the following section.

Accelerating the rsETH Unwind with E-Mode LT Reductions

rsETH loops sit in a dedicated E Mode category (“rsETH / ETH, wstETH, ETHx”), allowing their liquidation timeline to be shortened through targeted LT reductions without affecting other ETH loops on Core.

Rather than applying a single substantial LT reduction, the proposed approach uses a series of smaller adjustments, each calibrated against the health factors of remaining positions. This brings liquidation events forward incrementally while ensuring that no position becomes liquidatable immediately upon execution.

The process would follow a recurring cycle:

  1. Set the rsETH CAPO maxYearlyRatioGrowthPercent to 0%.
  2. Engagement window. Borrowers have time to unwind or migrate voluntarily.
  3. Assess the tightest remaining position. If it would reach HF < 1 within one month, make no change. Otherwise, reduce the E-Mode LT just enough to bring its projected liquidation to one month away.
  4. Wait for the liquidation and repeat Step 3 until no rsETH loops remain.

The first LT reduction is applied at the start of the cycle, once the engagement and migration window has closed. Its magnitude is determined by the health factors of the remaining positions at that point. Based on current positions, a reduction from 95% to 94.18% would bring the first projected liquidation forward from month 6 to month 1. However, as health factors continue to deteriorate under the 0% CAPO growth cap during the engagement window, the reduction required at the start of the cycle is expected to be smaller.

Following each liquidation episode, the next LT reduction is calibrated against the remaining positions using the same approach, bringing the next projected liquidation to one month ahead.

This approach ensures that each adjustment provides at least one month of notice before the next projected liquidation event. The interval can also be extended to accommodate available onchain liquidity and the beacon chain withdrawal queue.

Assuming passive borrowers, this iterative approach brings approximately 48% of rsETH collateral to liquidation within 12 months and approximately 72% within 24 months, compared with approximately 3% and 33%, respectively, under the CAPO adjustment alone.

Interaction with the ARFC’s migration path

The ARFC proposes adding wstETH, weETH and cbETH as collateral to the existing rsETH E Mode category, allowing borrowers to migrate their collateral without first repaying their WETH debt. We support this approach, as it provides borrowers with a straightforward migration path and facilitates the voluntary reduction of rsETH exposure.

However, subsequent E-Mode LT reductions would also affect positions that have already migrated to these assets, potentially penalizing borrowers who followed the proposed migration path. This needs to be addressed through appropriate sequencing of the migration and LT reduction processes.

This can be avoided by sequencing the migration and LT reduction processes:

  1. Migration window: Give rsETH borrowers time to swap their collateral into wstETH, weETH or cbETH within the rsETH E Mode category, as proposed in the ARFC.
  2. Move migrated positions to the standard ETH-correlated E Mode: Once migrated, borrowers can switch to the existing ETH-correlated E Mode, which has the same 93% / 95% LT / LTV parameters and WETH as a borrowable asset. This transition has no impact on their health factors.
  3. Begin the LT reduction cycle: Announce a fixed start date for the first LT reduction. By that point, the rsETH E-Mode category should contain only remaining rsETH positions, allowing subsequent LT reductions to target the intended exposure without affecting migrated borrowers.

This sequencing preserves the ARFC’s migration route while allowing the remaining rsETH loops to follow a shorter and more predictable unwinding timeline.

The DAO as Liquidator of Last Resort

In a worst case scenario with limited voluntary unwinding, the debt liquidated during these episodes may exceed available secondary market liquidity.

The DAO should therefore be prepared to fund these liquidations using treasury ETH and exit the seized rsETH through Kelp’s withdrawal queue.

Depending on the expected liquidation volume, the E-Mode liquidation bonus could also be increased ahead of each episode to compensate the DAO for the additional duration risk associated with holding seized rsETH until it can be redeemed through the withdrawal queue.

osETH Considerations

osETH shares the ETH correlated E-Mode with wstETH, weETH and cbETH. Therefore, E-Mode LT reductions cannot selectively target osETH positions without affecting other ETH loops. Setting maxYearlyRatioGrowthPercent to 0% on the osETH CAPO adapter remains the only targeted mechanism.

Overall Assessment

  • Targeted: CAPO adjustments affect only rsETH and osETH collateral valuations, leaving WETH borrowing costs and other ETH loops unchanged.
  • Predictable: The mechanism provides borrowers with time to unwind voluntarily, with liquidation timelines determined by individual position health factors.
  • Gradual: Borrowers can continue benefiting from the underlying exchange rate appreciation, but must progressively reduce leverage to maintain healthy positions.
  • Controlled market impact: Liquidations are distributed over time and occur partially, subject to the 50% close factor.
  • Accelerated rsETH unwind: E Mode LT reductions provide an additional mechanism to bring liquidation timelines forward without affecting other ETH loops, provided migrated positions are moved to the standard ETH correlated E Mode first.
  • Implementation: No new contracts or development are required. The analysis relies on updates to existing CAPO parameters and E Mode configuration.
  • Limitations: The rsETH CAPO adapter is currently shared across Aave V3 Core, V3 Prime and the V4 Kelp spoke. Should the CAPO adjustment be pursued, it could be scoped to the intended V3 markets by deploying a dedicated rsETH CAPO adapter and updating the corresponding oracle source, leaving other deployments that use the existing adapter unchanged. The treatment of other deployments is outside the scope of this analysis.

Conclusion and Potential Implementation Path

The following sequence combines the initial measures and migration path proposed in LlamaRisk’s ARFC with the targeted deleveraging mechanisms outlined in this analysis:

  1. Implement initial measures: Freeze osETH and set its LTV to 0%. rsETH is already frozen. Retain the ARFC’s proposed E-Mode additions to facilitate collateral migration.
  2. Apply CAPO adjustments: Set maxYearlyRatioGrowthPercent to 0% on the rsETH and osETH CAPO adapters.
  3. Engage and monitor: Work with issuers and the largest borrowers to facilitate voluntary migration and unwinding. Provide options to support borrowers, including tokenized positions in the beacon chain withdrawal queue and access to short term credit to bridge liquidity needs.
  4. Accelerate rsETH unwinding: Following the engagement and migration window, allow borrowers who have migrated to wstETH, weETH or cbETH to switch their positions to the standard “ETH correlated” E-Mode. Once migrated positions have exited the rsETH E-Mode, initiate the iterative LT reduction process for the remaining rsETH positions.
  5. Prepare for residual liquidations: Ensure the DAO is prepared to fund liquidations with treasury ETH where secondary market liquidity is insufficient, and exit seized rsETH and osETH through their respective withdrawal queues.

This analysis focuses solely on the CAPO parameter adjustments described in step 2. The subsequent measures, including the iterative E-Mode LT reductions for rsETH, will be reviewed separately and shared as needed.

governance_posts.description:
Summary

This ARFC proposes to update the collateral factors of the Coinbase tokenized equities on the Aave V4 Equities Hub on Base to the latest market data, under the current version of the collateral factor methodology. Most of the listed stocks have become more volatile since the start of 2026, and six of the eight reserves would move to a lower collateral factor. METAc and TSLAc would keep their current values. Maximum liquidation bonuses, liquidation fees, collateral risk, caps, and the USDC interest rate curve are unchanged.

Reserve Recent volatility, annualized Current Collateral Factor Proposed Collateral Factor
MSFTc 33.5% 79% 65%
AAPLc 25.0% 78% 65%
GOOGLc 38.3% 76% 65%
AMZNc 36.7% 73% 65%
NVDAc 43.4% 70% 65%
METAc 43.3% 65% 65%
TSLAc 49.2% 65% 65%
SPCXc 69.9% 55% 53%

Source: LlamaRisk and Aave, November 19, 2026

The new collateral factors would take effect as a new risk configuration on each of the six reserves. No position would be liquidated by the update.

Motivation

Stock volatility has risen since the start of 2026. The recent volatility of the typical S&P 500 stock, the geometric mean over the index members, has gone from 27.9% to 34.1% a year, and six of the seven stocks behind the Magnificent Seven (Mag7) tokens on the hub have followed, MSFT the most (19.4% to 33.5%) and AAPL the least (22.5% to 25.0%). TSLA, the most volatile of the seven, eased slightly, from 50.6% to 49.2%. Recent volatility weights each daily return more the more recent it is, with half the weight on the last 46 sessions.


Source: LlamaRisk, December 31, 2025 and November 19, 2026

The collateral factor of each reserve is derived from its stock’s recent volatility, and the proposed values are set on the latest data.

Collateral Factors

In Aave V4 the collateral factor is both the borrowing limit and the liquidation threshold. For a stock priced 24/5, it has to cover the largest fall from any off-hours price to the lowest price before five minutes past the next regular open, plus a 0.5% allowance for the feed’s deviation threshold. The haircut, the fall the collateral factor is built to absorb, is sized so that this fall exceeds it on one night per stock in ten years, with a 2020-type crash counted as one year in ten.

The haircut scales a forecast of the stock’s daily volatility over the next year by the size of a once-in-ten-years off-hours fall relative to daily volatility, measured across S&P 500 stocks. The forecast weights the stock’s recent moves and pulls them partly toward the market-wide level. The collateral factor is what remains after the haircut, the maximum liquidation bonus, and an allowance for interest while a position waits for liquidation, rounded down to a whole point and capped at 65%.

Reserve Recent volatility, annualized Haircut Max Liquidation Bonus Collateral Factor
MSFTc 33.5% 22.84% 5.50% 65%
AAPLc 25.0% 18.15% 5.50% 65%
GOOGLc 38.3% 25.42% 5.50% 65%
AMZNc 36.7% 24.56% 5.50% 65%
NVDAc 43.4% 28.09% 5.50% 65%
METAc 43.3% 28.05% 5.50% 65%
TSLAc 49.2% 30.99% 5.50% 65%
SPCXc 69.9% 42.51% 6.50% 53%

Source: LlamaRisk, November 19, 2026

The 65% maximum sets the collateral factor of MSFTc, AAPLc, GOOGLc, AMZNc, NVDAc, and METAc; at a 5.5% maximum liquidation bonus it corresponds to a minimum haircut of 31.25%. TSLAc’s haircut gives 65% directly. SPCXc is not an S&P 500 member, so its haircut uses the larger scale the method sets for stocks outside the index, and, with trading history since June 2026, its forecast leans more on the market-wide level. The interest allowance charges 24% a year over the longest market closure, 92 hours and 35 minutes, which is the top of the hub’s USDC rate curve; on SPCXc it includes the reserve’s 10% collateral risk.


Source: LlamaRisk and Aave, November 19, 2026

Implementation

The proposed collateral factors would be added as a new dynamic risk configuration on each of the six reserves, with their current maximum liquidation bonus and liquidation fee. In Aave V4 new positions open under the latest configuration, and an existing position moves to it when it borrows, withdraws, or changes the assets it uses as collateral; such an action goes through only if the position is healthy under the new collateral factors. No position would be liquidated by the update.

Specification

The update applies to the Mag-7 Spoke of the Equities Hub on Base. Collateral risk, caps, the dynamic liquidation bonus configuration, and the USDC interest rate curve are unchanged.
